title: Examining wayfinding behaviours in architectural spaces using brain imaging with electroencephalography (EEG)
research_question: To assess the effect of gender, age, level of education, and ceiling height on cognitive processing and wayfinding, and to investigate these effects on architectural design using a brain imaging method. Specifically, the study investigates: H.1: What effect does spatial design have on wayfinding behaviour? H.2: What is the effect of objects located in the designed space on the wayfinding behaviour of people? H.3: What is the effect of space height on wayfinding behaviour? H.4: Do factors such as education level and gender affect wayfinding behaviour?

participants.description: 343 healthy volunteers (3 female participants left during the experiment, so their data were removed, resulting in N=340). Age ranged from 18 to 65 years (average age men: 36.94, women: 34.76). Participants were instructed not to take any medication or use tobacco/alcohol the day before the experiment. Participants had no psychiatric condition or severe eye problems.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three virtual reality mazes (labyrinths) of identical plan layout (90 m²), materials, and colors, but varying in ceiling height: Space-I (3.5 m), Space-II (3 m), Space-III (2.5 m). Participants navigated using Samsung Gear VR-w/Controller.
2D plan layouts of the three mazes, showing start and end points, for initial memorization by participants.
30 different virtual objects (e.g., watches, mirrors, books, racks, vases, carpets, lighting elements, pictures) placed within the three mazes, used for object-space matching test.

measures.instrument: Time taken to exit each virtual maze (up to 240s limit)
Pedestrian Axe (PA) software generated axle maps, tracing movements and counting passes through corridors
Object-mapping test using Spatial Analyser software (matching objects to spaces seen)
Electroencephalography (EEG) measuring Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Theta waves in different brain regions
EEG wave patterns (e.g., Beta for anxiety, Theta for executive functions)

findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance (exit time from virtual mazes)
findings.quote: A significant relationship exists between participants' time of departure from the space (exit without being lost in the space) and education levels.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance (average exit time from virtual mazes)
findings.quote: men were clearly more successful than women, as shown in Figure 6.
Figure 10 shows that men have a higher recall rate than women.
those aged between 19-40 are more successful in both male and female groups than older participants.
The most unsuccessful group seems to be between 40 and 65 years of age for both men and women.
The axle maps of the participants aged 0-18 years are quite 'clean' compared to those in the age range of 40-65 years.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding behavior (passing the same place multiple times)
findings.mechanism: needlessly navigate routes, making the route more complicated
findings.quote: Participants in the age range 40-65 passed the same place more often than those in the 0-18 age group
it is noticeable that, as age increases, the matching rate decreases.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance (exit time from virtual mazes)
findings.quote: an increase in level of education, regardless of gender, reduced the exit time from all three different labyrinths.
people with low levels of education have more difficulty finding their way.
Women participants with a low level of education scored especially low in the object-space matching test (less than 24%).
The average exit time from the highest ceiling (3.5 m) was 112 s
the average exit time from the space with the lowest ceiling height was 137 s.
Interestingly, both men and women were more successful at exiting a high-ceiling space.

Participants entered three spaces respectively and remembered the objects in the first space more clearly than in the others. The factor that contributes to this is thought to be the difference in ceiling height in the rooms.

findings.mechanism: information derived from some brain regions overworking
findings.quote: people who cannot find direction for a long period in a low-elevation environment become anxious on account of information derived from some brain regions overworking.
this study clearly showed that the height of the space exerted an influence on wayfinding behaviours, unlike the "form of the plan".
This study showed that objects placed in the space were effective in finding direction in the space.
It is thought that the converse is true: objects placed in the space changed wayfinding behaviours.

findings.mechanism: Beta activity is involved in decision-making
findings.quote: Beta waves also increased at critical decision points for directional behaviour.

findings.consequent: Theta wave activity in frontal lobe (EEG)
findings.mechanism: frontal lobe controls complex cognitive actions, executive functions, emotions and behaviours
findings.quote: Theta activity was observed in the frontal lobe at the beginning of navigation.
Examination of the 2D plan plane shows lower levels of Theta activity.

findings.consequent: Alpha wave activity in occipital lobe (EEG)
findings.mechanism: occipital lobe processes all visual information tasks and plays a role in object recognition
findings.quote: Occipital lobe activity through Alpha waves is more pronounced during wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Alpha wave activity in occipital lobes (EEG)
findings.quote: persons with high visual matching success showed more activity in the occipital lobes.
a temporary increase in Theta / Alpha activity was observed, an increase that is thought to be related to cognition and memory.

findings.antecedent: Seeing exit gate and completing task
findings.consequent: Beta wave activity in F3/F4 and Fz channels (EEG)
findings.quote: The brain waves of those participants who saw the exit gate and completed the task showed sudden increases in the F3 / F4 and Fz Beta waves, suggesting success or happiness.

findings.consequent: Theta band activity in pre-frontal cortex (EEG)
findings.quote: The Theta band in the pre-frontal cortex, in particular, was active in those who successfully completed the task.

findings.consequent: Theta wave activity in parietal lobe (EEG)
findings.mechanism: parietal lobe processes and receives sensory information by connecting all the senses; participants failed seem to be collecting different information from different senses, but could not turn this information into action.
findings.quote: In these participants, Theta waves were focussed in the parietal lobe and there was no frontal lobe activity.
Theta waves were focussed in the parietal lobe and there was no frontal lobe activity.

findings.antecedent: Being lost in room (women with secondary school education)
findings.consequent: Theta band activity in Fp1 and Fp2 channels (frontal lobe) (EEG)
findings.quote: The two graphs (Figures 13 and 14) show high values of Fp1 and Fp2 (frontal lobe) Theta band for the women with secondary school education, indicating anxiety and fear.

findings.mechanism: overdeveloped Beta waves create anxiety, making the person tense and aggressive, causing them to make incorrect decisions.
findings.quote: more Beta activity was detected during object-mapping, as was the case of being unable to find direction.

findings.consequent: Capacity to find direction and remember objects
findings.mechanism: interfered with their perception of the space
findings.quote: Increased Beta activity decreased the capacity of participants to find their direction and correctly remember objects in the environment, as it had interfered with their perception of the space.

mechanisms: Higher elevation creates a feeling of refreshment and comfort, which facilitates wayfinding and memory.
Low-elevation environments cause anxiety due to overworking of specific brain regions, hindering wayfinding.
Beta wave activity is involved in decision-making, but overdeveloped Beta waves (associated with anxiety/tension) interfere with perception and lead to incorrect decisions.
Theta activity in the frontal lobe is linked to complex cognitive actions, executive functions, and emotions during navigation.
Occipital lobe Alpha waves are involved in visual information processing and object recognition during wayfinding.

Parietal lobe processes and receives sensory information; when Theta waves are focused here during difficult wayfinding, it suggests participants are collecting information but cannot convert it into action.
implementation_implications: Planners and designers need to understand how physical attributes of the architectural environment, especially ceiling height, affect wayfinding performance.
The content of a space (e.g., objects) is as important as its plan organization for wayfinding.
Simpler spatial layouts with appropriate physical differentiation, particularly in terms of height, can improve wayfinding and spatial knowledge.
Virtual reality and brain imaging techniques (like EEG) can be used to test and refine designs, allowing for better control of physical factors and understanding human responses.
Architects should be sensitive to group understandings of the physical environment to shape spaces that improve quality of life.

tables.description: Demographic details of volunteers participating in the experiment, showing gender, age distribution, and education level.
Task duration according to gender and education level, showing average exiting times from first, second, and third spaces.
Level of significance between male and female participants in exit times from spaces, showing F-statistics, p-values, mean differences, and confidence intervals for each maze.

limitations: The study acknowledges socio-cultural implications of findings (e.g., gender and education differences) but does not delve into them.
The experiment was conducted in a virtual reality environment, which may have limitations in generalizability to real-world physical spaces (though efforts were made to make it realistic).
The study design used specific mazes, and while difficulty was controlled, the generalizability of findings to all architectural layouts may be limited.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Neural Correlates of Spatial Cognition (specifically theta oscillations)
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Frontal midline theta power is associated with cognitive load and successful wayfinding performance in virtual environments, reflecting processes like spatial memory and navigation.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how environmental features and cognitive processes are linked to neural activity (EEG) and ultimately wayfinding performance.
